title: Women
hook: the third order: marriage, divorce and vows

segments.voice: Yesterday, reading and fasting: Esther from the scroll, and a fast that points to changed works. Your line was reading and fasting. Today we leave the order of appointed times and open the third order. Day one thousand seventy-six.

The third order of the Mishnah has a one-word title: Nashim. Women. Open it expecting a book about women, and you'll find something else. A tractate on what happens when a husband dies childless. One on the marriage contract. One on vows. One on the nazirite, who promises to skip wine and let the hair grow. One on divorce, and one on how a marriage begins. What ties them together isn't a person. It's a promise. Today: the order of the Mishnah about the bonds people make with each other.
screen: `NASHIM: WOMEN.` → `MARRIAGE, VOWS, DIVORCE.` → `NOT A PERSON. A PROMISE.`

segments.voice: Nashim. Here's how the order works. First, it's about bonds you enter by your own words. A marriage begins with an act and words of acceptance. A vow begins when you say it. A divorce ends with a document. In each case, words create something real between two people. The Torah, speaking of vows, says, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation, "he shall not break his word; he shall do according to all that proceedeth out of his mouth." That verse could stand over the whole order. Second, why is it called Women? Because the world it describes is one where a man usually acted and a woman was acted upon. He gives the ring. He writes the divorce. Even the section of the Torah on vows, the one just quoted, goes on to discuss when a father or a husband may cancel a woman's vow. Some readers say that's part of why vows sit in this order at all. It's honest to say this plainly. The Mishnah was written in a world very different from today's, and its frame is a man's. Third, the rabbis also built protections inside that frame, and you'll meet some of them this week: a contract that guards a wife, a ruling that weeps over divorce, a long struggle for women who are left stranded. And Jews today live with this order in different ways. Orthodox communities keep its law and work within it, for example with prenuptial agreements. Conservative rabbis have added clauses and rulings. Reform and Reconstructionist Jews often reshape the ceremonies so both partners speak and give. What they share is the order's deepest claim. A promise between two people is holy ground. The Talmud even compares a bride to something set apart for the Temple. Covenants between people.
screen: `WORDS THAT MAKE A BOND.` · `A MAN'S FRAME, SAID PLAINLY.` · `PROTECTIONS INSIDE THE FRAME.` · `STREAMS LIVE IT DIFFERENTLY.` · then, large: `COVENANTS BETWEEN PEOPLE.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: think about one commitment you've made. Sit, and let your breath slow. It could be a marriage, a friendship, a promise to a parent or a child, a vow to yourself. Remember the words, if there were words. Where were you when you said them? Who heard? Now ask how that promise is doing. Is it being kept? Has it changed shape? Don't judge it. Just look at it, the way you'd look at something precious on a shelf. The bell holds the time.
Nashim. Women: the third order of the Mishnah, on marriage, divorce, vows and the promises that bind people. Today's word.
Your line: covenants between people. Today, before you promise anything, even a small yes, say it slowly, as words that make something real. Day one thousand seventy-six.

howItsDone: Jewish weddings, divorces and vows follow rules that grow out of this order; Orthodox communities apply them as halacha, Conservative rabbis apply them with their own rulings, and Reform and Reconstructionist couples often adapt the ceremonies so that both partners speak.
